elements.text: Making good progress again on node. I've stubbed in all of the "chaser" objects and implemented their initialization, destruction, and messaging. The design calls for each chaser on an independent strand, which allows them to perform long-running and expensive operations concurrently given enough threads. Each is registered to receive it's triggering event(s) via a subscriber which is retained by the
full_node

class, which operates on the network strand. Events are created by the other chasers. Protocols negotiate for objects (e.g. headers/txs/blocks) over the wire and submit these to chasers, which manage chain state, such as the tx pool (DAG) and header tree as well as the parallel block download queue. The submission of these objects to the appropriate chaser is the external trigger for chaser activity. Protocols also register for events, such as to broadcast a newly confirmed block/compact or accepted transaction and to download blocks that have been accepted via candidate headers messages.

elements.text: I've completed the concurrent header sync implementation. This adds  a "chaser" to maintain state across connections, where previously we could only run one connection at a time when syncing headers. The chaser maintains a "currency window" which is set to 60 minutes. Headers older than this are cached in a std lib hash table, along with their validation chain state (which gets stored in the database with each header). When a header chain is both "strong" (more work than the database candidate chain) and "current", the headers from the hash table are moved to the store, and these and any that were not previously in the strong branch are "candidated" (ordered into the candidate chain). This is like block confirmation in the "confirmed" chain, except that the candidate chain is the strongest valid *header* chain available. This is always at least as strong as the confirmed chain and they are usually the same. I just noticed a startup on 10 peers where we went from process startup with empty store to fully-populated and validated candidate chain (831,014 headers) in 17 seconds. Anything under a minute is pretty reasonable given that we don't optimize peer connections (drop slow ones) when syncing headers, as we don't want to prioritize large/fast peers. It's been up and running for a few days with no issues, performing both the initial header sync and ongoing updates in the same logic.

elements.text: Blocks-first works just like v3. It can be run by hardwiring it enabled despite headers-first protocol version (required for most peers out there). Took a few days to do blocks first, which preserved the feature of being able to operate at any configured protocol and/or fork levels.

elements.text: Yesterday I took a short detour to implement the longstanding objective of chain "milestones" (avoiding another mixed metaphor, as a checkpoints and a milestones are on roads - though not "chains" mind you), as well as minimum chain work.

text: Yesterday I took a short detour to implement the longstanding objective of chain "milestones" (avoiding another mixed metaphor, as a checkpoints and a milestones are on roads - though not "chains" mind you), as well as minimum chain work.

elements.text: Since milestones exist to mark a known place on the road, but not force you through it (unlike a checkpoint) they are just perf optimizations. They are only useful for headers first, and cannot optimize headers (though that is not in need of it). So once a header reaches that point the blocks under it do not require validation (presumption of previous verification by the node owner). This implies only one is necessary, since block download won't start anyway until headers are "current" (top is recent in time).

elements.text: So when a strong header chain is both current and minimum work is satisfied, or a given header is  a checkpoint or milestone, the header chain is written to disk as the candidate chain. This is the same for "initial/catch-up" and ongoing sync. And when a header passes through a milestone or checkpoint, all hash-corresponding blocks under it bypass validation.

elements.text: minimum chain work is fine as long as it's not configured by developers, but versions of bitcoind ship with preconfigured values. This could allow that configuration to reject the valid chain, resulting in a stall - a soft fork. The code doesn't determine these, it's done by developers. So this will remain configurable and should really default to top checkpoint work. In any case it's done.

elements.text: It doesn't really solve low work DoS, it just prevents it from being written to disk. It can still blow up our header RAM cache (std::unordered_map). But a restart resolves that, and more can be done to manage that later.
